props.title: Duel in the Sun
props.initialSlug: Epic Western ignites forbidden interracial passion

sections.content: Duel in the Sun stands as David O. Selznick's ambitious attempt to recreate the epic scope of Gone with the Wind (1939), resulting in a sexually-charged Western melodrama that pushed boundaries for its time. Nicknamed "Lust in the Dust," the film's torrid romance between Jennifer Jones's Pearl Chavez and Gregory Peck's Lewt McCanles sparked controversy and censorship battles. The film's saturated Technicolor photography by Lee Garmes and Ray Rennahan created a fever-dream aesthetic that influenced later Western auteurs like Sergio Leone in Once Upon a Time in the West (1968).

sections.content: Director King Vidor brought operatic intensity to the proceedings, establishing a template for the "psychological Western" that would flourish in the 1950s. The film's exploration of racial prejudice, through Pearl's mixed heritage and the town's treatment of her, predated more overt social commentary Westerns like Broken Arrow (1950). Selznick's excessive production style, including multiple directors and writers, resulted in a sometimes uneven but unforgettable epic that cost $6 million - an astronomical sum for 1946.

The film's influence extends beyond its controversial elements. The climactic duel sequence, with its expressionistic use of color and dramatic rock formations, established new possibilities for Western action choreography. Later films like The Searchers (1956) would build on its integration of landscape and psychological drama. Jennifer Jones's performance as Pearl - alternating between refined lady and "half-wild" creature - challenged Hollywood's traditional depiction of women in Westerns. sections.content: Duel in the Sun marked a crucial transition point between classical Westerns and more complex postwar variations. Its frank treatment of desire and racial identity opened doors for films like The Ox-Bow Incident (1943) and High Noon (1952) to tackle serious themes within the genre framework. The film's excessive style influenced European directors, particularly the Italian Western movement of the 1960s, where directors like Sergio Leone and Sergio Corbucci embraced similarly operatic approaches to the genre.
